sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is Git and why is it used?

Git is a distributed version control system that records snapshots of a project over time, so you can see what changed, when, by whom and why, and return to any earlier state. It is used because it makes two otherwise hard things routine: several people editing the same codebase without overwriting each other, and experimenting on a branch without risking the working version. Every modern deployment pipeline is triggered by Git, which is why it is the one tool essentially every developer and operator shares.
What is the difference between Git and GitHub?

Git is the version control software that runs on your machine and does all the actual work. Committing, branching, merging, storing history. GitHub is a commercial website that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features Git does not have: pull requests, issues, code review, permissions and CI. Git works completely without GitHub, and GitLab, Bitbucket and self-hosted alternatives provide the same role. Confusing the two is common because most people meet Git through GitHub.
What does "distributed" mean in distributed version control?

Every clone is a complete repository, with the full history and every branch, rather than a thin checkout of a central server. That has three practical consequences: nearly every operation, log, diff, branch, commit, is local and therefore instant, you can work entirely offline and sync later, and there is no single point of failure because every clone is effectively a backup. Centralised systems such as SVN keep history only on the server, which is why they needed a connection for operations Git does in milliseconds.
Does Git store a copy of every file in every commit?

Conceptually yes. Each commit references a complete snapshot of the tree. Physically no: Git stores each unique piece of content once, addressed by its SHA-1 hash, so a file unchanged across a thousand commits is stored once and referenced a thousand times. It later repacks objects into compressed packfiles that store deltas between similar ones. This is why a repository with years of history is often smaller than the working directory it produced.
Do I need to know Git to work in DevOps?

Yes, and not merely to store code. Infrastructure as code, pipeline definitions, Kubernetes manifests and configuration all live in Git, and GitOps goes further by making the repository the declared desired state of production. That means a Git revert can be a rollback, a branch protection rule can be a deployment control, and a commit message can be the audit record for a change. Git fluency is closer to a prerequisite than a skill in this field.
What are the main Git terms a beginner needs?

Six carry most of the weight. A repository is the project plus its complete history. A commit is one recorded snapshot with a message and a parent. A branch is a movable pointer to a commit, which is why creating one is instant. HEAD is where you currently are. A remote is another copy of the repository, conventionally named origin. The staging area is the draft of your next commit, and it is the concept that makes the add-then-commit two-step make sense.

## Introduction & Overview

Learn what Git is and why version control matters: distributed versus centralized systems, how Git stores history and the key terms to know first.

## What Is Git?

Git is a version control system that tracks changes to files over time. It is most often used for source code, but it can track almost any text-based project. Instead of saving files as final-v2-really-final.txt, Git stores a history of changes so you can see what changed, who changed it, and when it changed.

In practice, Git lets you work safely. You can experiment, undo mistakes, compare versions, and collaborate with other people without constantly copying folders by hand.

Tip: Think of Git as a timeline for your project. Every important save point becomes part of a history you can inspect and reuse later.

## Why Version Control Matters

Without version control, teams run into familiar problems:

Git solves these problems by recording snapshots called commits. Each commit has an ID, message, author, and timestamp. Because Git stores history, you can answer useful questions like:

Imagine you change a deployment script and production starts failing. With Git, you can compare the current script to the previous commit and quickly spot the mistake:

That is far safer than guessing or restoring random backup files.

```bash
git log --oneline
git diff HEAD~1 HEAD -- deploy.sh
```

## How Git Stores History

Git does not track “the latest file only.” It stores snapshots of your project over time. When you create a commit, Git records the state of tracked files at that moment.

A simple workflow looks like this:

Later, after editing the file again:

Now you have two checkpoints. You can inspect either version whenever needed.

```bash
git init
git add app.js
git commit -m "Add initial app file"
```

## Git vs Other Version Control Systems

Git is not the only version control system. Older tools include Subversion (SVN), Mercurial, and CVS.

Here is a practical comparison:

Git became popular because it is fast, reliable, and excellent at branching and merging. Modern platforms such as GitHub, GitLab, and Bitbucket also made Git collaboration easier.

Teams often choose Git because it supports:

## Centralized vs Distributed Version Control

The biggest conceptual difference is between centralized and distributed systems.

In a centralized system, there is one main server with the official history. Developers check files in and out from that server.

Git is a distributed version control system. Every clone contains the full repository history, not just the latest files.

Note: Even though Git is distributed, teams usually still use a shared remote repository such as GitHub as the collaboration hub.

## Git in Everyday DevOps Work

Git is not only for application code. DevOps teams use it for:

This matters because change history is critical in operations. If a deployment pipeline breaks, Git helps you trace the exact configuration change that caused it.

## Key Terms to Remember

A repository or repo is the project folder Git tracks, including its history.

A commit is a saved snapshot of tracked changes.

A branch is an independent line of work, often used for features or fixes.

A clone is a full local copy of a repository.

A remote is a shared repository location, such as one hosted on GitHub.

## What You Should Remember

Git helps you manage change safely. It gives you history, accountability, collaboration, and the confidence to experiment without losing work. Compared with older centralized tools, Git gives every developer a full local history and makes branching much easier.

If you remember one idea, remember this: Git is not just a backup tool. It is a system for working with change in a controlled, reviewable way.

Identify the Git feature that makes offline history inspection and local commits possible.

Scenario: A teammate keeps saving files as deploy-final-v3-really-final.sh to track changes manually.

Question: What Git concept from this tutorial directly solves that problem?

Choose the Git concept that replaces manual file versioning with structured history.

Scenario: A deployment pipeline started failing after a recent configuration edit.

Question: According to the tutorial, why is Git especially useful in this DevOps situation?

Pick the reason Git helps trace a broken pipeline or infrastructure change.

It is used because it makes two otherwise hard things routine: several people editing the same codebase without overwriting each other, and experimenting on a branch without risking the working version. Every modern deployment pipeline is triggered by Git, which is why it is the one tool essentially every developer and operator shares.

What is the difference between Git and GitHub?

Git is the version control software that runs on your machine and does all the actual work. Committing, branching, merging, storing history. GitHub is a commercial website that hosts Git repositories and adds collaboration features Git does not have: pull requests, issues, code review, permissions and CI. Git works completely without GitHub, and GitLab, Bitbucket and self-hosted alternatives provide the same role. Confusing the two is common because most people meet Git through GitHub.

What does "distributed" mean in distributed version control?

Every clone is a complete repository, with the full history and every branch, rather than a thin checkout of a central server. That has three practical consequences: nearly every operation, log, diff, branch, commit, is local and therefore instant, you can work entirely offline and sync later, and there is no single point of failure because every clone is effectively a backup. Centralised systems such as SVN keep history only on the server, which is why they needed a connection for operations Git does in milliseconds.

Conceptually yes. Each commit references a complete snapshot of the tree. It later repacks objects into compressed packfiles that store deltas between similar ones. This is why a repository with years of history is often smaller than the working directory it produced.

Do I need to know Git to work in DevOps?

Yes, and not merely to store code. Infrastructure as code, pipeline definitions, Kubernetes manifests and configuration all live in Git, and GitOps goes further by making the repository the declared desired state of production. That means a Git revert can be a rollback, a branch protection rule can be a deployment control, and a commit message can be the audit record for a change. Git fluency is closer to a prerequisite than a skill in this field.

What are the main Git terms a beginner needs?

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: How do I check whether Git is already installed?

git --version prints the version if it is present. On macOS this can be misleading: the command may exist and trigger a prompt to install the Xcode Command Line Tools, or report an Apple-shipped build that lags well behind upstream. which git tells you where it came from, /usr/bin/git is Apple's, /opt/homebrew/bin/git or /usr/local/bin/git is Homebrew's. Install via Homebrew if you want current Git on a Mac.
What is the first thing to configure after installing Git?

Your identity, because Git refuses to commit without it and it is stamped permanently into every commit you make: git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email "you@example.com". Use the email associated with your hosting account, or your commits will not be attributed to you. Then set init.defaultBranch main to match what GitHub and GitLab expect, and core.editor to something you can exit.
Why does Git say "Please tell me who you are"?

No user.name or user.email is configured, so Git cannot author a commit. Set them globally with the two --global commands, or per repository without the flag when a project needs a different address. The error usually appears on a brand new machine, or after cloning into a repository with a local config that cleared the values. Commits already made under the wrong identity can be corrected with git commit --amend --reset-author, though only safely before pushing.
Should I install Git with Homebrew or use the version macOS ships?

Homebrew, if you use Git seriously. The Apple-supplied build is tied to Xcode Command Line Tools updates and is often several minor versions behind, which means missing newer commands and flags, git switch and git restore arrived relatively recently, for example. brew install git gives you current Git that updates with everything else you have installed. Make sure Homebrew's path precedes /usr/bin in your PATH so the new one actually wins.
What is the difference between Git for Windows and Git in WSL?

They are two separate installations that do not share configuration or credentials. Git for Windows provides Git Bash and integrates with Windows tooling; Git inside a WSL distribution is a Linux Git operating on the Linux filesystem. Mixing them causes real problems, line endings, file permissions and credential helpers all differ, so pick one per project and stay with it. If you develop inside WSL, use WSL's Git and keep repositories in the Linux filesystem rather than under /mnt/c, which is also much faster.
How should I handle line endings across Windows, macOS and Linux?

Add a .gitattributes file to the repository with * text=auto so Git normalises text files to LF in history while checking them out natively, plus explicit rules for files that must stay LF, *.sh text eol=lf in particular, since a shell script with CRLF fails inside a Linux container with a baffling "not found". Committing .gitattributes is better than relying on each person's core.autocrlf setting, because it makes the behaviour a property of the project rather than of whoever cloned it.

installing-git.markdown:
## Why Installation and Setup Matter

Installing **Git** is quick, but good initial configuration saves time every day. Your name and email appear in commits, your editor opens when Git needs input, and your default branch name affects new repositories.

A clean setup helps you avoid confusing commit authors, awkward editor prompts, and inconsistent branch names across projects.

> **Tip:** Configure Git once on your machine before starting real work. It prevents small problems from becoming repeated annoyances.

## Installing Git on macOS

On macOS, the easiest path is often to install the Xcode Command Line Tools. If Git is missing, macOS may prompt you automatically when you run `git`.

Check first:

```bash
git --version
```

If Git is not installed, you can use:

```bash
xcode-select --install
```

If you use Homebrew, you can also install Git with:

```bash
brew install git
```

After installation, verify it:

```bash
git --version
```

## Installing Git on Linux

Git is available through most Linux package managers.

### Ubuntu or Debian

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install git -y
```

### Fedora

```bash
sudo dnf install git -y
```

### CentOS or RHEL

```bash
sudo yum install git -y
```

### Arch Linux

```bash
sudo pacman -S git
```

Then confirm the installation:

```bash
git --version
```

## Installing Git on Windows

On Windows, the most common option is **Git for Windows**, which includes Git Bash and useful command-line tools.

1. Download Git for Windows from the official installer.
2. Run the installer.
3. Accept the defaults unless your team has specific requirements.
4. Open **Git Bash** or Command Prompt and verify:

```bash
git --version
```

Git Bash is especially helpful because many tutorials and DevOps commands assume a Unix-like shell experience.

> **Note:** If you work with VS Code, Git for Windows integrates well with its built-in terminal and source control features.

## Configuring Your Identity

Git needs to know who you are so commits can record an author.

Set your global name:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Vish Patel"
```

Set your global email:

```bash
git config --global user.email "vish@example.com"
```

These settings apply to all repositories on your machine unless a repository overrides them.

Check your current config:

```bash
git config --global --list
```

### Why This Matters

If your name or email is wrong, your commits may appear under the wrong identity on Git hosting platforms. That can make collaboration and auditing harder.

## Setting Your Default Editor

Git sometimes opens an editor for commit messages, merge messages, or rebase instructions. Setting your preferred editor makes those workflows smoother.

For VS Code:

```bash
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
```

For Vim:

```bash
git config --global core.editor "vim"
```

For Nano:

```bash
git config --global core.editor "nano"
```

The `--wait` flag is important for VS Code because Git must pause until you finish editing.

## Choosing a Default Branch Name

Many teams now use `main` instead of `master` as the default branch name.

Configure new repositories to start with `main`:

```bash
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```

Now when you run `git init`, the initial branch will be `main`.

Verify it:

```bash
git config --global init.defaultBranch
```

## Useful Optional Setup

Here are a few optional settings beginners often appreciate.

### Show Helpful Colors

```bash
git config --global color.ui auto
```

### Cache Credentials Temporarily on macOS or Linux

```bash
git config --global credential.helper cache
```

### Use the Windows Credential Manager

On Windows, Git for Windows can help manage stored credentials depending on your install options.

> **Tip:** Be careful storing credentials directly in files. Use secure credential helpers or SSH keys when possible.

## Local vs Global Configuration

Git configuration can exist at different levels:

- **System**: applies to every user on a machine
- **Global**: applies to your user account
- **Local**: applies only inside one repository

For example, if one work project needs a company email, you can override it inside that repository:

```bash
git config user.email "vish@company.com"
```

To inspect all effective settings and where they came from:

```bash
git config --list --show-origin
```

## A Good First-Time Setup Checklist

A practical first-time setup often looks like this:

```bash
git config --global user.name "Vish Patel"
git config --global user.email "vish@example.com"
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global color.ui auto
```

Then verify:

```bash
git config --global --list
```

## What You Should Remember

Installing Git is easy, but the important part is configuration. Set your identity, editor, and default branch right away. That gives you cleaner commits, better compatibility with team workflows, and fewer surprises when Git opens an editor or creates a new repository.

Once Git is installed and configured, you are ready to create or clone repositories and start tracking real work.

  }}

### Exercise 2: Choosing an editor

**Question:** Why does the tutorial recommend `git config --global core.editor "code --wait"` when using VS Code?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{
    id: 'git-installing-q2',
    title: 'Exercise 2: Choosing an editor',
    description: 'Identify why the --wait flag matters when configuring VS Code as the Git editor.',
    options: [
      { id: 'a', text: 'It makes Git open a browser tab instead of the terminal.' },
      { id: 'b', text: 'It forces every commit to use squash merge mode.' },

      { id: 'd', text: 'It changes the default branch name to code.' },
    ],
    correctId: 'c',
    explanation: 'Git sometimes needs you to write commit messages or edit rebase instructions. The `--wait` flag tells Git to pause until VS Code is closed for that editing session, so the workflow can complete correctly.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      a: 'The setting is about editor behavior for Git prompts, not about launching a browser.',
      b: 'Editor configuration does not control merge strategy choices like squash merging.',
      d: 'Default branch naming is handled by `init.defaultBranch`, not by `core.editor`.',
    },
  }}
/>

### Exercise 3: Global vs local identity

**Scenario:** Your personal machine uses `vish@example.com` globally, but one company repository must use `vish@company.com` for commits.

**Question:** Which approach matches the tutorial?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{
    id: 'git-installing-q3',
    title: 'Exercise 3: Global vs local identity',
    description: 'Choose the correct way to override commit identity for just one repository.',
    options: [
      { id: 'a', text: 'Reinstall Git separately for the company repository.' },
      { id: 'b', text: 'Change the system config so every user on the machine uses the company email.' },
      { id: 'c', text: 'Create a new default branch called company and commit there.' },
      { id: 'd', text: 'Run `git config user.email "vish@company.com"` inside that repository.' },

    correctId: 'd',

    wrongExplanations: {

      b: 'System config is much broader than needed and would affect other users or repositories.',
      c: 'Branch names do not control commit author metadata.',

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How do I check whether Git is already installed?**

`git --version` prints the version if it is present. On macOS this can be misleading: the command may exist and trigger a prompt to install the Xcode Command Line Tools, or report an Apple-shipped build that lags well behind upstream. `which git` tells you where it came from, `/usr/bin/git` is Apple's, `/opt/homebrew/bin/git` or `/usr/local/bin/git` is Homebrew's. Install via Homebrew if you want current Git on a Mac.

**What is the first thing to configure after installing Git?**

Your identity, because Git refuses to commit without it and it is stamped permanently into every commit you make: `git config --global user.name "Your Name"` and `git config --global user.email "you@example.com"`. Use the email associated with your hosting account, or your commits will not be attributed to you. Then set `init.defaultBranch main` to match what GitHub and GitLab expect, and `core.editor` to something you can exit.

**Why does Git say "Please tell me who you are"?**

No `user.name` or `user.email` is configured, so Git cannot author a commit. Set them globally with the two `--global` commands, or per repository without the flag when a project needs a different address. The error usually appears on a brand new machine, or after cloning into a repository with a local config that cleared the values. Commits already made under the wrong identity can be corrected with `git commit --amend --reset-author`, though only safely before pushing.

**Should I install Git with Homebrew or use the version macOS ships?**

Homebrew, if you use Git seriously. The Apple-supplied build is tied to Xcode Command Line Tools updates and is often several minor versions behind, which means missing newer commands and flags, `git switch` and `git restore` arrived relatively recently, for example. `brew install git` gives you current Git that updates with everything else you have installed. Make sure Homebrew's path precedes `/usr/bin` in your `PATH` so the new one actually wins.

**What is the difference between Git for Windows and Git in WSL?**

They are two separate installations that do not share configuration or credentials. Git for Windows provides Git Bash and integrates with Windows tooling; Git inside a WSL distribution is a Linux Git operating on the Linux filesystem. Mixing them causes real problems, line endings, file permissions and credential helpers all differ, so pick one per project and stay with it. If you develop inside WSL, use WSL's Git and keep repositories in the Linux filesystem rather than under `/mnt/c`, which is also much faster.

**How should I handle line endings across Windows, macOS and Linux?**

Add a `.gitattributes` file to the repository with `* text=auto` so Git normalises text files to LF in history while checking them out natively, plus explicit rules for files that must stay LF, `*.sh text eol=lf` in particular, since a shell script with CRLF fails inside a Linux container with a baffling "not found". Committing `.gitattributes` is better than relying on each person's `core.autocrlf` setting, because it makes the behaviour a property of the project rather than of whoever cloned it.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between git add and git commit?

git add moves changes into the staging area, which is a draft of your next commit. git commit records whatever is staged as a permanent snapshot in history. The two-step design is the point: you can edit ten files and commit them as three logical commits by staging selectively, which makes history readable and reverting precise. git add -p takes this further, letting you stage individual chunks within a single file.
What is the difference between git init and git clone?

git init turns an existing directory into a new repository with no history and no remote. You use it once, when starting something from scratch. git clone <url> copies an existing remote repository, bringing its full history and automatically configuring origin so git push and git pull work immediately. If you init when you meant to clone, you end up with an empty repository and have to add the remote by hand with git remote add origin <url>.
How do I see what changed before committing?

git diff shows changes you have not staged, and git diff --staged shows what you have staged, that second one is the real pre-commit review, because it is exactly what the commit will contain. git status gives the file-level overview of both. A useful habit is git diff --staged immediately before every commit; it catches stray debug statements and accidentally staged files more reliably than any hook.
How do I unstage a file I added by mistake?

git restore --staged <file> removes it from the staging area while keeping your edits in the working directory. The older equivalent is git reset HEAD <file>, which you will still see in documentation and which does the same thing. If you want to discard the edits as well, git restore <file> does that, and it is not recoverable, since those changes were never recorded anywhere, so check git diff first.
What does git log show and how do I make it readable?

By default it prints every commit with full hash, author, date and message, which is a lot of screen for little information. git log --oneline gives one commit per line, and git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate adds the branch structure, which is the single most useful way to understand what state a repository is in. git log -p <file> shows the actual changes to one file over time, and git log --since="2 weeks ago" narrows the range.
Why does git commit open an editor, and how do I avoid it?

Because no message was supplied, so Git asks for one. Passing -m "your message" writes it inline and skips the editor, which is what most people use day to day. If the editor opens and you are stuck in Vim, :wq saves and :q! aborts the commit. Set something you know with git config --global core.editor "code --wait" for VS Code or "nano" for nano. Reserve the editor for commits that deserve a body explaining why, which -m makes awkward.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between git switch and git checkout?

git checkout does several unrelated jobs, moving between branches, creating them, and restoring files, which made it a common source of accidents, since git checkout <file> silently discarded changes. Git split those responsibilities: git switch changes branches and git restore restores files. git switch -c <name> replaces git checkout -b <name>. Both new commands are stable and preferred in new work; checkout still functions and is not going away, so older documentation remains valid.
What does "detached HEAD" mean and how do I fix it?

HEAD normally points at a branch name, which in turn points at a commit. When you check out a commit, tag, or remote-tracking branch directly, HEAD points straight at that commit with no branch attached, that is detached. You can look around and even commit, but those commits belong to no branch and become unreachable once you leave. If you have made commits you want to keep, git switch -c <new-branch> right where you are captures them. If you have not, git switch main returns you to normal.
How do I delete a local and a remote branch?

git branch -d <name> deletes a local branch and refuses if it holds commits not merged anywhere, which is a safety net worth keeping; -D forces it. For the remote, git push origin --delete <name>. Deleting a remote branch does not remove other people's stale local copies of it. They need git fetch --prune, or git config --global fetch.prune true to have it happen automatically on every fetch.
How do I rename a Git branch?

git branch -m <new-name> renames the branch you are on, or git branch -m <old> <new> for another one. Renaming a branch that exists on the remote takes three steps, because the remote branch is a separate reference: rename locally, push the new name with git push origin -u <new-name>, then delete the old one with git push origin --delete <old-name>. Anyone else working on it needs to re-point their local branch, so agree the change first.
What is a good branch naming convention?

Use a short prefix that says what kind of change it is, then a brief description in kebab-case: feature/user-search, fix/login-redirect, chore/bump-deps. Many teams add the ticket number, feature/PROJ-412-user-search, which lets tooling link branches to issues automatically. Keep them lowercase and avoid spaces and unusual characters, since branch names become part of URLs and filesystem paths. The value is not aesthetic: a consistent scheme makes git branch --list 'fix/*' and automated cleanup possible.
Does creating a branch in Git copy all my files?

No, and this is why Git branching is fast where older systems were slow. A branch is a 41-byte file containing a commit hash. A pointer, nothing more. Creating one writes that file and does not touch your working directory at all, which is why git switch -c is instant even in a huge repository. Switching branches then updates only the files that actually differ between the two commits.

git-branching.markdown:
## What a Branch Really Is

A **branch** in Git is a movable pointer to a commit. Instead of copying your whole project into a new folder, Git lets you create a lightweight branch and continue work there.

This is one of Gitâs biggest strengths. You can build a feature, fix a bug, or test an idea without disturbing the main line of development.

> **Tip:** A branch is not a second copy of the project. It is a label that points to a specific place in commit history.

## Why Branching Matters

Imagine the `main` branch contains stable application code. You want to add a login page, but the work may take several commits. Instead of changing `main` directly, you create a feature branch.

Benefits of branching:

- isolate work in progress
- reduce risk to stable code
- make code reviews easier
- support multiple parallel changes

In real teams, short-lived feature branches are common because they keep the shared branch clean.

## Viewing Branches

To list local branches:

```bash
git branch
```

The current branch is marked with `*`.

To see both local and remote branches:

```bash
git branch -a
```

A typical result might be:

```bash
* main
  feature/login
  remotes/origin/main
```

## Creating a Branch

Create a new branch called `feature/login`:

```bash
git branch feature/login
```

This creates the branch, but you stay on your current branch until you switch.

To create and switch in one step, use:

```bash
git switch -c feature/login
```

Older tutorials may use `git checkout -b feature/login`, which still works, but `git switch` is clearer for branch changes.

## Switching Between Branches

Move to an existing branch:

```bash
git switch main
```

Switch back:

```bash
git switch feature/login
```

When you switch branches, Git updates your working directory to match the selected branchâs latest commit.

### Real Example

```bash
git switch -c feature/navbar
echo "Add navigation" >> README.md
git add README.md
git commit -m "Document navbar plan"
git switch main
```

After switching back to `main`, that change is no longer visible there because it belongs to the feature branch.

## Understanding HEAD

**HEAD** is Gitâs way of saying âyour current position.â Most of the time, HEAD points to the branch you are currently on.

If you are on `main`, HEAD points to `main`, and `main` points to the latest commit on that branch.

You can inspect recent history with:

```bash
git log --oneline --decorate -5
```

You may see output like:

```bash
7fa12cd (HEAD -> feature/login) Add login form markup
1ab93e0 (main) Create app skeleton
```

That means HEAD currently points to `feature/login`.

## Deleting a Branch

After a branch has been merged and is no longer needed, delete it to keep the repository tidy.

Delete a fully merged branch safely:

```bash
git branch -d feature/login
```

Force delete a branch that has unmerged commits:

```bash
git branch -D feature/login
```

> **Note:** Use `-D` carefully. It can remove a branch pointer before its work is merged elsewhere.

## Detached HEAD Explained

A **detached HEAD** happens when HEAD points directly to a commit instead of a branch.

For example:

```bash
git checkout 1ab93e0
```

Now you are no longer âonâ `main` or `feature/login`. You are looking at a specific past commit.

This can be useful for inspection, testing, or reproducing an old state. But if you make commits here, they are not attached to a branch unless you create one.

### Safe Way to Continue from Detached HEAD

If you decide to keep that work, create a branch immediately:

```bash
git switch -c investigate-old-release
```

That gives the new commits a proper branch name and keeps them easy to find.

## Good Branch Naming Habits

Teams usually prefer simple, descriptive names such as:

- `feature/login-page`
- `fix/pipeline-timeout`
- `docs/git-tutorial`
- `hotfix/rollback-script`

A good branch name helps everyone understand the purpose of the work.

## A Practical Branch Workflow

Here is a realistic beginner workflow:

```bash
git switch main
git pull
git switch -c feature/add-footer
echo "Footer content" >> index.html
git add index.html
git commit -m "Add footer to homepage"
git switch main
```

At this point, `main` stays stable while the new work lives on `feature/add-footer` until it is reviewed and merged.

## What You Should Remember

Branches are lightweight and powerful. Use them to isolate work, protect stable code, and make collaboration easier. HEAD represents your current location in history. Most of the time it points to a branch, but during detached HEAD it points directly to a commit.

If you remember one best practice, remember this: create a branch before doing meaningful new work.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the difference between git switch and git checkout?**

`git checkout` does several unrelated jobs, moving between branches, creating them, and restoring files, which made it a common source of accidents, since `git checkout <file>` silently discarded changes. Git split those responsibilities: `git switch` changes branches and `git restore` restores files. `git switch -c <name>` replaces `git checkout -b <name>`. Both new commands are stable and preferred in new work; `checkout` still functions and is not going away, so older documentation remains valid.

**What does "detached HEAD" mean and how do I fix it?**

`HEAD` normally points at a branch name, which in turn points at a commit. When you check out a commit, tag, or remote-tracking branch directly, `HEAD` points straight at that commit with no branch attached, that is detached. You can look around and even commit, but those commits belong to no branch and become unreachable once you leave. If you have made commits you want to keep, `git switch -c <new-branch>` right where you are captures them. If you have not, `git switch main` returns you to normal.

**How do I delete a local and a remote branch?**

`git branch -d <name>` deletes a local branch and refuses if it holds commits not merged anywhere, which is a safety net worth keeping; `-D` forces it. For the remote, `git push origin --delete <name>`. Deleting a remote branch does not remove other people's stale local copies of it. They need `git fetch --prune`, or `git config --global fetch.prune true` to have it happen automatically on every fetch.

**How do I rename a Git branch?**

`git branch -m <new-name>` renames the branch you are on, or `git branch -m <old> <new>` for another one. Renaming a branch that exists on the remote takes three steps, because the remote branch is a separate reference: rename locally, push the new name with `git push origin -u <new-name>`, then delete the old one with `git push origin --delete <old-name>`. Anyone else working on it needs to re-point their local branch, so agree the change first.

**What is a good branch naming convention?**

Use a short prefix that says what kind of change it is, then a brief description in kebab-case: `feature/user-search`, `fix/login-redirect`, `chore/bump-deps`. Many teams add the ticket number, `feature/PROJ-412-user-search`, which lets tooling link branches to issues automatically. Keep them lowercase and avoid spaces and unusual characters, since branch names become part of URLs and filesystem paths. The value is not aesthetic: a consistent scheme makes `git branch --list 'fix/*'` and automated cleanup possible.

**Does creating a branch in Git copy all my files?**

No, and this is why Git branching is fast where older systems were slow. A branch is a 41-byte file containing a commit hash. A pointer, nothing more. Creating one writes that file and does not touch your working directory at all, which is why `git switch -c` is instant even in a huge repository. Switching branches then updates only the files that actually differ between the two commits.

git-merging.markdown:
## What Merging Does

**Merging** combines changes from one branch into another. It is how feature work eventually becomes part of `main` or another shared branch.

A common example is merging `feature/login` into `main` after the feature is complete and reviewed.

```bash
git switch main
git merge feature/login
```

Git tries to combine history automatically. When histories fit together cleanly, merging is easy. When the same lines changed in different ways, you may get a conflict that needs manual resolution.

## Fast-Forward Merge

A **fast-forward merge** happens when the target branch has not moved since the feature branch was created. Git can simply move the branch pointer forward.

Imagine this sequence:

- `main` at commit A
- create `feature/docs`
- add commits B and C on `feature/docs`
- `main` still points at A

Merging can look like this:

```bash
git switch main
git merge feature/docs
```

Git may respond with a fast-forward update because there is no need to create a separate merge commit.

### Why It Happens

The histories form a straight line. `main` can just âcatch upâ to the feature branch.

Benefits:

- simple history
- fewer merge commits
- easy to understand for small projects

## Three-Way Merge

A **three-way merge** happens when both branches moved forward independently.

For example:

- `main` has commit D
- `feature/login` has commits B and C
- both branches share an earlier common ancestor A

Now Git must combine two lines of development. It creates a new merge commit that has two parents.

```bash
git switch main
git merge feature/login
```

This is called a three-way merge because Git compares:

- the common ancestor
- the current branch tip
- the branch being merged

## When Teams Use `--no-ff`

By default, Git may fast-forward when possible. Some teams prefer to always keep a visible merge commit for feature branches.

Use:

```bash
git switch main
git merge --no-ff feature/login
```

This forces a merge commit even if a fast-forward would work.

### Why Use `--no-ff`?

It can make history easier to read because the branch integration remains visible as a single merge event. That can help when reviewing past work or reverting an entire feature.

> **Tip:** Teams that rely heavily on pull requests often like explicit merge commits because they preserve the story of how a feature entered the main branch.

## What a Merge Conflict Is

A **merge conflict** happens when Git cannot decide how to combine changes automatically.

This usually occurs when:

- both branches changed the same lines
- one branch deleted a file the other edited
- file renames and edits overlap in confusing ways

Git will pause the merge and ask you to resolve the conflict manually.

## Step-by-Step Conflict Resolution

Assume both branches edited the same line in `app.conf`.

Start the merge:

```bash
git switch main
git merge feature/config-update
```

Git may report a conflict. Check the status:

```bash
git status
```

Open the conflicted file. You may see markers like this:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
port=8080
=======
port=9090
>>>>>>> feature/config-update
```

### What the Markers Mean

- `<<<<<<< HEAD` shows the version from the current branch
- `=======` separates the two versions
- `>>>>>>> feature/config-update` shows the incoming version

### Resolve the File

Choose the correct final content, for example:

```text
port=9090
```

Or combine both ideas if needed. Then stage the resolved file:

```bash
git add app.conf
```

Complete the merge:

```bash
git commit
```

Git usually opens your editor with a default merge message.

## Verifying the Merge

After merging, inspect the history:

```bash
git log --oneline --graph --decorate -10
```

This helps you confirm whether Git created a fast-forward result or a merge commit.

You can also test the application after resolving conflicts:

```bash
npm test
```

Or if it is a shell-based project:

```bash
./run-checks.sh
```

Validation matters because a âcleanâ merge is not automatically a correct merge.

## Abort a Problematic Merge

If you start a merge and realize you are not ready, you can often stop and return to the pre-merge state:

```bash
git merge --abort
```

This is helpful if you accidentally merged the wrong branch or want to review changes before trying again.

> **Note:** `git merge --abort` works best before you make extra manual changes beyond the merge conflict state.

## Merge vs Rebase at a High Level

Merging preserves the true branch structure. Rebasing rewrites commits onto a new base to create a straighter history. Both are useful, but merge is often the safer beginner choice because it does not rewrite existing commits.

## What You Should Remember

Merging is how Git combines branches. A fast-forward merge simply moves a pointer. A three-way merge creates a merge commit when histories diverged. Conflicts happen when Git cannot safely decide between competing changes, and resolving them means editing the affected files, staging the results, and finishing the merge.

Use `--no-ff` when your team wants feature integrations to remain clearly visible in history.

## Test Your Understanding

### Exercise 1: Recognizing a fast-forward

**Scenario:** `main` is still at commit A, while `feature/docs` moved from A to B to C and nothing new was added to `main`.

**Question:** What kind of merge should Git usually be able to perform when you merge `feature/docs` into `main`?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{
    id: 'git-merging-q1',
    title: 'Exercise 1: Recognizing a fast-forward',
    description: 'Identify the merge type when the target branch has not moved since branching.',
    options: [
      { id: 'a', text: 'A detached HEAD merge, because main is too old to merge.' },
      { id: 'b', text: 'A conflict-only merge, because every feature branch must create a conflict.' },
      { id: 'c', text: 'A fast-forward merge, because Git can move the main pointer straight to C.' },
      { id: 'd', text: 'A revert merge, because main must undo A before accepting B and C.' },
    ],
    correctId: 'c',
    explanation: 'The lesson defined a fast-forward merge as the case where the target branch has not advanced independently. Git can simply move `main` forward to the feature tip because the history is still a straight line.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      a: 'Detached HEAD is about checkout state, not this merge shape.',
      b: 'Conflicts happen only when Git cannot combine competing changes automatically.',
      d: 'Revert is for undoing commits, not for normal branch integration.',
    },
  }}
/>

### Exercise 2: Preserving feature history

**Question:** Why might a team choose `git merge --no-ff feature/login` even when a fast-forward merge is possible?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{
    id: 'git-merging-q2',
    title: 'Exercise 2: Preserving feature history',
    description: 'Pick the reason teams force a merge commit with --no-ff.',
    options: [
      { id: 'a', text: 'It skips code review and merges more quickly.' },
      { id: 'b', text: 'It keeps a visible merge commit so the feature integration remains clear in history.' },
      { id: 'c', text: 'It prevents the branch from ever being deleted.' },
      { id: 'd', text: 'It rewrites the feature branch into a linear rebase automatically.' },
    ],
    correctId: 'b',
    explanation: 'The tutorial explained that `--no-ff` forces a merge commit so the feature arrival stays visible as a single event. Teams often like that because it makes reviews, audits, and full-feature reverts easier to understand later.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      a: 'Merge strategy does not eliminate the need for review.',
      c: 'Branch deletion is a separate cleanup decision after the merge.',
      d: 'Rebase and merge are different workflows. `--no-ff` does not transform a merge into a rebase.',
    },
  }}
/>

### Exercise 3: Finishing conflict resolution

**Scenario:** A merge stopped with conflict markers in `app.conf`. You edited the file so the final content is correct.

**Question:** According to the tutorial, what should you do next to complete the merge workflow?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{
    id: 'git-merging-q3',
    title: 'Exercise 3: Finishing conflict resolution',
    description: 'Choose the next step after manually resolving merge conflict markers.',
    options: [
      { id: 'a', text: 'Run `git clone` to create a clean copy before saving the merge.' },
      { id: 'b', text: 'Delete the incoming branch immediately so Git assumes the conflict is fixed.' },
      { id: 'c', text: 'Run `git merge --abort` even though the file is already resolved.' },
      { id: 'd', text: 'Stage the resolved file with `git add app.conf`, then complete the merge commit.' },
    ],
    correctId: 'd',
    explanation: 'The lesson showed that after you resolve the conflict markers, you stage the corrected file so Git knows the conflict is handled. Then you complete the merge, typically with `git commit` if Git has not already created the final commit message step for you.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      a: 'Cloning again does not mark the conflict as resolved in the current repository.',
      b: 'Deleting a branch does not resolve the merge state or record the final content.',
      c: 'Abort is for cancelling the merge, not for finishing a conflict you already resolved.',
    },
  }}
/>

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**How do I resolve a Git merge conflict?**

Open each file Git lists as conflicted and find the `<<<<<<<`, `=======` and `>>>>>>>` markers. The section above `=======` is the branch you are on, the section below is the branch you are merging in. Edit the file into the state you actually want, often a combination of both, not a choice between them, delete all three markers, then `git add` the file and `git commit`. `git status` tracks which files are still outstanding, and `git diff --name-only --diff-filter=U` lists just the unresolved ones.

**What is the difference between a fast-forward and a three-way merge?**

A fast-forward happens when the target branch has no commits since you branched off, so Git simply moves the pointer forward to your latest commit, no merge commit, and history stays linear. A three-way merge happens when both branches have moved on, so Git combines them using the common ancestor plus each tip, and records the result as a merge commit with two parents. You cannot choose: Git fast-forwards whenever it can, unless you pass `--no-ff` to force a merge commit.

**When should I use git merge --no-ff?**

When you want the branch to remain visible in history. `--no-ff` forces a merge commit even where a fast-forward was possible, so the graph shows that a group of commits belonged to one feature and `git log --graph` reads as a series of merged branches. That makes reverting a whole feature easy, one `git revert -m 1` on the merge commit, and it is why many teams enable it for release branches. The cost is a busier graph, which is why other teams prefer squash merges instead.

**How do I abort a merge and start over?**

`git merge --abort` returns you to the state before the merge began, discarding partial resolutions. It works while the merge is in progress, that is, before you commit, which covers the case where the conflicts turn out to be more than you expected. If you have already committed the merge, use `git reset --hard HEAD~1` to drop it locally, and `git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>` if it has already been pushed, since resetting a shared branch strands everyone else.

**What does "Already up to date" mean when merging?**

Every commit on the branch you are merging is already reachable from your current branch, so there is nothing to bring in. The usual cause is not having fetched: your local copy of the remote branch is stale, and Git is telling you the truth about what it knows. Run `git fetch` first, then merge. The other cause is merging the wrong direction. Merging `main` into your feature branch when you meant to merge your feature into `main`.

**Should my team use merge commits, squash merges, or rebase merges?**

Squash merges suit most teams: each pull request becomes one commit on `main`, so history reads as a list of shipped changes and reverting is trivial, at the cost of losing the individual commits. Merge commits preserve everything and keep the branch visible, which matters when you need the full record for audit or bisecting inside a feature. Rebase merges give a linear history with every commit kept, which is tidy but rewrites hashes. Pick one and enforce it in the repository settings rather than leaving it per-developer.

sections.title: What Rebase Does
paragraphs: Rebase moves or reapplies commits onto a new base commit. Instead of combining two branches with a merge commit, rebase rewrites the branch so it appears to start from a later point in history.
Suppose feature/login was created from main, but main has advanced since then. Rebasing feature/login onto main replays the feature branch commits on top of the newer main.
This can make history look cleaner and more linear.
Tip: Rebase rewrites commit history. That is powerful, but it means you should be careful with commits other people are already using.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between git rebase and git merge?

Both integrate one branch into another; they differ in what history they leave behind. git merge creates a merge commit joining the two lines of development, preserving exactly what happened including the fact that work happened in parallel. git rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch, producing a straight line as though you had started from the latest code. Merge is honest about history and clutters the graph; rebase is tidy and rewrites commit hashes. Most teams rebase local feature branches before opening a pull request, then merge the result.
Is it safe to rebase a branch that has been pushed?

Only if you are the only person working on it. Rebasing creates new commits with new hashes, so the remote branch and your local one diverge and git push is rejected until you force it. Use git push --force-with-lease rather than --force: it refuses the push if someone else has added commits you have not seen, which turns silent data loss into an error message. Never rebase a shared branch such as main. Everyone who has pulled it will be stranded on commits that no longer exist.
How do I squash multiple commits into one?

Run git rebase -i HEAD~n where n is how many commits back you want to go, then change pick to squash (or s) on every commit except the first. The first stays pick because the others are folded into it. Git then opens an editor to combine the messages. If you only want the first commit's message, use fixup instead of squash to discard the others. Many platforms also offer "Squash and merge" on a pull request, which achieves the same result without rebasing locally.
How do I get out of a rebase that has gone wrong?

git rebase --abort returns the branch to exactly where it was before the rebase started, at any point during the process. That is the escape hatch to reach for whenever you are unsure. If the rebase has already completed and you want the old state back, git reflog lists where HEAD has been, and git reset --hard HEAD@{n} moves you to the entry before the rebase. The reflog is why a completed rebase is recoverable and why "I lost my work" is almost never actually true.
Why do I keep hitting the same conflict repeatedly during a rebase?

Because a rebase replays each commit in turn, so a line you changed in several commits conflicts once per commit. Resolve the file, git add it, then git rebase --continue to move to the next one. Two things help: squashing related commits before rebasing so there are fewer replays, and enabling git config --global rerere.enabled true, which records how you resolved a conflict and reapplies that resolution automatically the next time the identical conflict appears.
What does git pull --rebase do and should I use it?

It fetches the remote branch and replays your local commits on top of it, instead of creating a merge commit. Without it, a plain git pull on a branch that has moved on both sides produces a "Merge branch 'main' of ..." commit, and a busy repository fills with them. Setting git config --global pull.rebase true makes it the default and keeps history linear. It is safe for your own unpushed commits, which is exactly what git pull is dealing with.

git-rebasing.markdown:
## What Rebase Does

**Rebase** moves or reapplies commits onto a new base commit. Instead of combining two branches with a merge commit, rebase rewrites the branch so it appears to start from a later point in history.

Suppose `feature/login` was created from `main`, but `main` has advanced since then. Rebasing `feature/login` onto `main` replays the feature branch commits on top of the newer `main`.

```bash
git switch feature/login
git rebase main
```

This can make history look cleaner and more linear.

> **Tip:** Rebase rewrites commit history. That is powerful, but it means you should be careful with commits other people are already using.

## Why Developers Rebase

Common reasons to use rebase include:

- updating a feature branch with the latest `main`
- cleaning up commit history before a pull request
- squashing many small commits into one logical commit
- reordering or editing recent commits

Rebase does not add new project content by itself. It changes how commits are arranged in history.

## Basic Rebase Example

Imagine this history:

- `main`: A â B â C
- `feature/login`: A â D â E

After rebasing `feature/login` onto `main`, the feature becomes:

- `main`: A â B â C
- `feature/login`: A â B â C â D' â E'

The apostrophes matter. Git usually creates new commit IDs because it is replaying the changes, not simply moving old commits.

Use:

```bash
git switch feature/login
git rebase main
```

If everything applies cleanly, you get the same code changes on a newer base.

## Rebase Conflicts

Rebase can produce conflicts just like merge. When that happens, Git pauses and asks you to resolve them.

A typical flow looks like this:

```bash
git rebase main
git status
```

Edit the conflicted file, remove conflict markers, then continue:

```bash
git add app.js
git rebase --continue
```

If another conflict appears, repeat the process.

If you want to stop and return to the original state:

```bash
git rebase --abort
```

## Interactive Rebase with `-i`

**Interactive rebase** lets you edit a series of recent commits. It is one of the most useful cleanup tools in Git.

To review the last three commits:

```bash
git rebase -i HEAD~3
```

Git opens your editor with something like:

```text
pick a1b2c3d Add login form
pick d4e5f6g Fix typo in login form
pick h7i8j9k Update login button color
```

You can change the action for each commit.

### Common Interactive Actions

- `pick`: keep the commit as is
- `reword`: keep the content but edit the message
- `edit`: pause so you can modify the commit
- `squash`: combine this commit with the previous one
- `drop`: remove the commit

## Squashing Commits

Suppose your history contains several tiny âfix typoâ commits that belong with the main feature. Interactive rebase can combine them.

Example:

```text
pick a1b2c3d Add login form
squash d4e5f6g Fix typo in login form
squash h7i8j9k Update login button color
```

After saving, Git combines the commits and lets you write a final commit message.

This is useful before opening a pull request because reviewers often prefer a clean, logical commit history.

> **Note:** Squashing is best used on your own unpublished work. Avoid rewriting shared history unless your team explicitly agrees on that workflow.

## Rebase vs Merge

Both rebase and merge combine lines of development, but they tell the story differently.

| Topic | Merge | Rebase |
|------|-------|--------|
| History shape | Preserves branch structure | Creates a more linear history |
| New commit IDs | Usually no rewrite of existing commits | Rewrites rebased commits |
| Safety for shared history | Safer | Needs more care |
| Typical use | Integrating branches | Cleaning history or updating a feature branch |

### Simple Rule of Thumb

- Use **merge** when you want to preserve real branch history
- Use **rebase** when you want a cleaner branch history before integration

## A Safe Team Habit

A common safe habit is:

1. Rebase your own feature branch onto the latest `main`
2. Push the updated branch
3. Merge it through a pull request

Example:

```bash
git switch main
git pull
git switch feature/login
git rebase main
git push --force-with-lease
```

`--force-with-lease` is safer than plain `--force` because it checks whether the remote changed in unexpected ways.

## What You Should Remember

Rebase replays commits onto a new base, which can make history look cleaner. Interactive rebase is especially useful for rewording, reordering, or squashing recent commits. But because rebase rewrites history, it should be used carefully on shared branches.

If you are unsure, use merge. If you want a polished branch before review, rebase can be a great tool.

## Test Your Understanding

### Exercise 1: Understanding rebased commits

**Scenario:** Your feature branch had commits D and E, and you rebased it onto a newer `main` with commits A, B, and C.

**Question:** Why did the tutorial show the rebased branch as `A -> B -> C -> D' -> E'` instead of keeping the old D and E exactly?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{
    id: 'git-rebasing-q1',
    title: 'Exercise 1: Understanding rebased commits',
    description: 'Identify why rebased commits usually receive new identities.',
    options: [
      { id: 'a', text: 'Because rebase replays the changes on a new base, which usually creates new commit IDs.' },
      { id: 'b', text: 'Because Git deletes the original changes and replaces them with merge commits only.' },
      { id: 'c', text: 'Because rebasing works only if the feature branch becomes a tag first.' },
      { id: 'd', text: 'Because Git must rename commits whenever the branch name contains a slash.' },
    ],
    correctId: 'a',
    explanation: 'Rebase does not merely move a pointer. It reapplies each commit onto a new base, so the resulting commits are usually new objects with new IDs even if the code changes look similar.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      b: 'That describes a different history shape. Rebase is replay, not automatic merge-commit replacement.',
      c: 'Tags are unrelated to whether a branch can be rebased.',
      d: 'Branch naming has nothing to do with commit identity changes during rebase.',
    },
  }}
/>

### Exercise 2: Cleaning up tiny commits

**Scenario:** Your feature branch contains `Add login form`, `Fix typo in login form`, and `Update login button color` as three small related commits.

**Question:** Which interactive rebase action from the tutorial is designed to combine the later two into the first logical commit?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{
    id: 'git-rebasing-q2',
    title: 'Exercise 2: Cleaning up tiny commits',
    description: 'Choose the interactive rebase action that combines related commits.',
    options: [
      { id: 'a', text: 'drop' },
      { id: 'b', text: 'reword' },
      { id: 'c', text: 'squash' },
      { id: 'd', text: 'pick' },
    ],
    correctId: 'c',
    explanation: 'The tutorial used `squash` to combine smaller follow-up commits into the previous commit. That is a common way to turn a noisy branch into a cleaner, more reviewable history before opening or updating a pull request.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      a: 'drop removes a commit entirely, which is different from combining it with another commit.',
      b: 'reword changes the message while keeping the commit content separate.',
      d: 'pick leaves the commit as-is with no combination at all.',
    },
  }}
/>

### Exercise 3: Pushing a rebased branch safely

**Question:** After rebasing your own feature branch onto the latest `main`, why did the tutorial recommend `git push --force-with-lease` instead of plain `--force`?

<MCQExercise
  exercise={{
    id: 'git-rebasing-q3',
    title: 'Exercise 3: Pushing a rebased branch safely',
    description: 'Pick the reason force-with-lease is safer after a history rewrite.',
    options: [
      { id: 'a', text: 'It converts the rebase into a merge if the branch contains conflicts.' },
      { id: 'b', text: 'It checks whether the remote changed unexpectedly before overwriting it.' },
      { id: 'c', text: 'It automatically restores dropped commits from the reflog on the server.' },
      { id: 'd', text: 'It prevents commit IDs from changing during the rebase.' },
    ],
    correctId: 'b',
    explanation: 'Because rebase rewrites branch history, the push usually must replace the remote branch tip. `--force-with-lease` adds a safety check so you do not overwrite remote work that changed since your last fetch.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      a: 'It does not change the workflow from rebase to merge.',
      c: 'The flag is a safety guard on push, not a remote recovery mechanism.',
      d: 'Commit IDs already changed during the rebase. The push flag does not prevent that.',
    },
  }}
/>

---

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the difference between git rebase and git merge?**

Both integrate one branch into another; they differ in what history they leave behind. `git merge` creates a merge commit joining the two lines of development, preserving exactly what happened including the fact that work happened in parallel. `git rebase` replays your commits on top of the target branch, producing a straight line as though you had started from the latest code. Merge is honest about history and clutters the graph; rebase is tidy and rewrites commit hashes. Most teams rebase local feature branches before opening a pull request, then merge the result.

**Is it safe to rebase a branch that has been pushed?**

Only if you are the only person working on it. Rebasing creates new commits with new hashes, so the remote branch and your local one diverge and `git push` is rejected until you force it. Use `git push --force-with-lease` rather than `--force`: it refuses the push if someone else has added commits you have not seen, which turns silent data loss into an error message. Never rebase a shared branch such as `main`. Everyone who has pulled it will be stranded on commits that no longer exist.

**How do I squash multiple commits into one?**

Run `git rebase -i HEAD~n` where `n` is how many commits back you want to go, then change `pick` to `squash` (or `s`) on every commit except the first. The first stays `pick` because the others are folded into it. Git then opens an editor to combine the messages. If you only want the first commit's message, use `fixup` instead of `squash` to discard the others. Many platforms also offer "Squash and merge" on a pull request, which achieves the same result without rebasing locally.

**How do I get out of a rebase that has gone wrong?**

`git rebase --abort` returns the branch to exactly where it was before the rebase started, at any point during the process. That is the escape hatch to reach for whenever you are unsure. If the rebase has already completed and you want the old state back, `git reflog` lists where `HEAD` has been, and `git reset --hard HEAD@{n}` moves you to the entry before the rebase. The reflog is why a completed rebase is recoverable and why "I lost my work" is almost never actually true.

**Why do I keep hitting the same conflict repeatedly during a rebase?**

Because a rebase replays each commit in turn, so a line you changed in several commits conflicts once per commit. Resolve the file, `git add` it, then `git rebase --continue` to move to the next one. Two things help: squashing related commits before rebasing so there are fewer replays, and enabling `git config --global rerere.enabled true`, which records how you resolved a conflict and reapplies that resolution automatically the next time the identical conflict appears.

**What does git pull --rebase do and should I use it?**

It fetches the remote branch and replays your local commits on top of it, instead of creating a merge commit. Without it, a plain `git pull` on a branch that has moved on both sides produces a "Merge branch 'main' of ..." commit, and a busy repository fills with them. Setting `git config --global pull.rebase true` makes it the default and keeps history linear. It is safe for your own unpushed commits, which is exactly what `git pull` is dealing with.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?

git fetch downloads commits and updates your remote-tracking branches such as origin/main, and changes nothing in your working directory. It is always safe to run. git pull is fetch followed immediately by a merge (or rebase) into your current branch, so it does alter your files and can produce conflicts. The useful habit is git fetch then git log origin/main..main to see what diverged before deciding how to integrate it, rather than letting pull decide for you.
How do I fix "rejected, non-fast-forward" when pushing?

The remote branch has commits you do not have locally, so accepting your push would discard them. Run git pull --rebase to replay your work on top of theirs, resolve any conflicts, then push. Do not reach for git push --force, which deletes their commits. If you genuinely must overwrite, after an intentional rebase of your own feature branch, use git push --force-with-lease, which refuses the push if the remote has moved since you last fetched.
What does git push -u origin main actually do?

-u (short for --set-upstream) records origin/main as the upstream of your local main, in addition to pushing. That association is what lets you type bare git push, git pull and git status afterwards and have Git know which remote branch you mean, including the "your branch is ahead by 2 commits" line in git status. You need it once per branch; after that the plain commands work. git branch -vv shows which branches have an upstream set.
Why don't I see a colleague's new branch?

Your local copy of the remote's branch list is only updated when you fetch. Run git fetch (or git fetch --all for every remote) and then git branch -r lists the remote branches you know about. The reverse problem is stale entries for branches that have been deleted upstream, which git fetch --prune clears; git config --global fetch.prune true makes that automatic on every fetch.
What is the difference between origin and upstream?

They are just remote names, not Git concepts. origin is the conventional name for the repository you cloned from, set automatically by git clone. upstream is the convention in fork-based workflows for the original project you forked: origin is your fork and upstream is the source. That is what makes git fetch upstream && git rebase upstream/main the standard way to bring a fork up to date. Add it with git remote add upstream <url>, and git remote -v lists what you have.
How do I change a remote's URL, for example from HTTPS to SSH?

git remote set-url origin git@github.com:user/repo.git, then confirm with git remote -v. This is the usual fix when HTTPS pushes start asking for a password that no longer works. GitHub stopped accepting account passwords for Git operations, so HTTPS needs a personal access token while SSH uses your key. Switching to SSH avoids the credential prompt entirely once your key is added to the account.

git-remote.markdown:
## What a Remote Is

A **remote** is a reference to a repository hosted somewhere else, usually on a platform such as GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. It gives your local repository a way to exchange commits with shared repositories.

The most common remote name is `origin`.

Check your current remotes:

```bash
git remote -v
```

You might see:

```bash
origin  https://github.com/example/devops-notes.git (fetch)
origin  https://github.com/example/devops-notes.git (push)
```

## Adding and Removing Remotes

If you started a repository locally and later created a hosted repository, add a remote like this:

```bash
git remote add origin https://github.com/example/devops-notes.git
```

Verify it:

```bash
git remote -v
```

To remove a remote:

```bash
git remote remove origin
```

To rename a remote:

```bash
git remote rename origin upstream
```

> **Tip:** In fork-based workflows, `origin` often points to your fork, while `upstream` points to the original project.

## Downloading Information with `git fetch`

`git fetch` downloads new commits and remote references without changing your working files.

```bash
git fetch origin
```

This updates your knowledge of remote branches such as `origin/main`, but it does not merge them into your current branch.

### Why `fetch` Is Safe

Because it does not change your working branch automatically, `fetch` is a safe way to inspect remote changes before deciding what to do next.

You can compare local and remote history after fetching:

```bash
git log --oneline main..origin/main
```

## Bringing Changes In with `git pull`

`git pull` is essentially a `fetch` followed by integration, usually a merge.

```bash
git pull origin main
```

If your current branch tracks a remote branch, you can often just run:

```bash
git pull
```

Be aware that pull can change your working tree immediately, which is why many developers prefer to `fetch` first when they want more control.

## Sending Changes Out with `git push`

Use `git push` to send local commits to a remote repository.

```bash
git push origin main
```

If you are pushing a new branch for the first time:

```bash
git push -u origin feature/login
```

The `-u` flag sets the **upstream** relationship, which means future pushes and pulls can use shorter commands.

## Tracking Branches and Upstream

A **tracking branch** is a local branch linked to a remote branch. This relationship makes commands like `git pull` and `git push` more convenient.

When you run:

```bash
git push -u origin feature/login
```

Git remembers that your local `feature/login` branch tracks `origin/feature/login`.

You can inspect tracking details with:

```bash
git branch -vv
```

Sample output:

```bash
* feature/login 3f91ab2 [origin/feature/login] Add login validation
  main          1de2049 [origin/main] Update README
```

## Setting Upstream Manually

If the branch already exists remotely, set the upstream manually:

```bash
git branch --set-upstream-to=origin/feature/login
```

Now simple `git pull` and `git push` commands work as expected from that branch.

## Common Remote Workflow

A typical day might look like this:

```bash
git switch main
git fetch origin
git pull origin main
git switch -c feature/update-docs
# make changes
git add .
git commit -m "Improve Git tutorial examples"
git push -u origin feature/update-docs
```

This sequence updates local `main`, creates a feature branch, and publishes it to the remote for review.

## Troubleshooting Common Confusion

### âWhy Donât I See Remote Changes?â

You may need to fetch first:

```bash
git fetch origin
```

### âWhy Did `git pull` Change My Files?â

Because pull integrates remote changes into your current branch. Use `fetch` first if you want to inspect before updating.

### âWhy Does Git Ask Me for an Upstream?â

Your local branch is not yet linked to a remote branch. Push with `-u` or set the upstream manually.

> **Note:** Authentication for push operations may use HTTPS tokens or SSH keys depending on your platform setup.

## What You Should Remember

Remotes connect your local repository to shared repositories. `git remote` manages the connection, `git fetch` downloads information safely, `git pull` downloads and integrates changes, and `git push` publishes your commits. Tracking branches and upstream settings reduce repetitive typing and make collaboration smoother.

If you are unsure whether you want your working tree changed, fetch first.

## Test Your Understanding

### Exercise 1: Inspecting before integrating

**Scenario:** You want to see what changed on `origin/main` before your current branch is modified.

**Question:** Which command from the tutorial is the safest first step?

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is the difference between git fetch and git pull?**

`git fetch` downloads commits and updates your remote-tracking branches such as `origin/main`, and changes nothing in your working directory. It is always safe to run. `git pull` is `fetch` followed immediately by a merge (or rebase) into your current branch, so it does alter your files and can produce conflicts. The useful habit is `git fetch` then `git log origin/main..main` to see what diverged before deciding how to integrate it, rather than letting `pull` decide for you.

**How do I fix "rejected, non-fast-forward" when pushing?**

The remote branch has commits you do not have locally, so accepting your push would discard them. Run `git pull --rebase` to replay your work on top of theirs, resolve any conflicts, then push. Do not reach for `git push --force`, which deletes their commits. If you genuinely must overwrite, after an intentional rebase of your own feature branch, use `git push --force-with-lease`, which refuses the push if the remote has moved since you last fetched.

**What does git push -u origin main actually do?**

`-u` (short for `--set-upstream`) records `origin/main` as the upstream of your local `main`, in addition to pushing. That association is what lets you type bare `git push`, `git pull` and `git status` afterwards and have Git know which remote branch you mean, including the "your branch is ahead by 2 commits" line in `git status`. You need it once per branch; after that the plain commands work. `git branch -vv` shows which branches have an upstream set.

**Why don't I see a colleague's new branch?**

Your local copy of the remote's branch list is only updated when you fetch. Run `git fetch` (or `git fetch --all` for every remote) and then `git branch -r` lists the remote branches you know about. The reverse problem is stale entries for branches that have been deleted upstream, which `git fetch --prune` clears; `git config --global fetch.prune true` makes that automatic on every fetch.

**What is the difference between origin and upstream?**

They are just remote names, not Git concepts. `origin` is the conventional name for the repository you cloned from, set automatically by `git clone`. `upstream` is the convention in fork-based workflows for the original project you forked: `origin` is your fork and `upstream` is the source. That is what makes `git fetch upstream && git rebase upstream/main` the standard way to bring a fork up to date. Add it with `git remote add upstream <url>`, and `git remote -v` lists what you have.

**How do I change a remote's URL, for example from HTTPS to SSH?**

`git remote set-url origin git@github.com:user/repo.git`, then confirm with `git remote -v`. This is the usual fix when HTTPS pushes start asking for a password that no longer works. GitHub stopped accepting account passwords for Git operations, so HTTPS needs a personal access token while SSH uses your key. Switching to SSH avoids the credential prompt entirely once your key is added to the account.

paragraphs: What is the difference between git stash apply and git stash pop?

Both restore the stashed changes to your working directory. pop then deletes the stash entry; apply leaves it in the list. Use apply when you want to put the same work onto more than one branch, or when you are not yet sure the restore will go cleanly, if it conflicts badly you still have the stash to fall back on. Does git stash include untracked files?

No, and this surprises people regularly. A plain git stash leaves new files sitting in your working directory, so switching branches carries them along and a "clean" stash turns out not to be. Use git stash -u (or --include-untracked) to include them, and git stash -a (--all) to include ignored files as well. Because -a sweeps up build output and node_modules, it is rarely what you want.
How do I see what is in a stash before restoring it?

git stash list shows the entries with their references. git stash show stash@{0} gives a summary of changed files, and git stash show -p stash@{0} prints the full diff. You can also restore a single file from a stash without applying the whole thing: git checkout stash@{0} -- path/to/file. Naming stashes as you create them, git stash push -m "half-done search filter", makes the list readable a week later, which the default WIP on main messages do not.
I dropped a stash by accident. Can I recover it?

Usually yes. A dropped stash is an unreachable commit, and git fsck --unreachable | grep commit lists candidates you can inspect with git show <sha>. Once you find it, git stash apply <sha> restores the contents. It works until Git garbage-collects, which is typically not for weeks. The wider lesson is that stashes are the least durable place to keep work. A throwaway commit on a scratch branch is recoverable through the reflog and cannot be dropped by a stray git stash clear.
How do I apply a stash to a different branch?

Just switch branches and apply it. Stashes are not tied to the branch they were created on. git switch other-branch then git stash pop is a standard way to move work you started in the wrong place. Conflicts are possible if the branches have diverged in the same files, and git checkout --theirs/--ours plus normal conflict resolution applies. If you expect trouble, use apply rather than pop so the stash survives a failed attempt.
When should I use a branch instead of a stash?

Whenever the work will outlive the next half hour. A stash is an unnamed, unordered pile that is easy to forget and easy to clear, and git stash list after a busy fortnight is nobody's friend. For anything you intend to return to, commit it on a branch, even as a scrappy "wip" commit you later amend or squash. Stash is at its best for exactly what it was designed for: parking a few minutes of work to pull, switch branch for a quick fix, or check something on a clean tree.
