git-aliases-config.markdown:
## Why Git Configuration Matters

Git works immediately, but a small amount of configuration makes daily work much smoother. Good defaults reduce mistakes, remove repeated typing, and help keep your environment consistent across projects.

In this lesson, you will cover:

- config scopes
- identity settings
- editor and default branch setup
- useful aliases
- a global ignore file

> **Tip:** Start with a few settings you use every day. You do not need a giant `.gitconfig` to get real value.

## Understanding `.gitconfig` Scopes

Git reads settings from three main levels:

- **system**: for all users on the machine
- **global**: for your user account
- **local**: for one repository only

Most personal preferences belong in **global** config, while project-specific exceptions belong in **local** config.

Useful commands:

```bash
git config --list
git config --list --show-origin
```

Typical files are:

- `/etc/gitconfig`
- `~/.gitconfig`
- `.git/config`

Local settings override global ones, and global settings override system ones.

## Setting Name and Email

Git writes author information into each commit, so configure identity first.

```bash
git config --global user.name "Vishvesh Patel"
git config --global user.email "vishvesh@example.com"
```

Verify the values:

```bash
git config --global user.name
git config --global user.email
```

If one repository needs a different email, set it locally:

```bash
cd company-project
git config user.email "vishvesh@company.com"
```

## Default Editor and Default Branch

Git may open an editor for commit messages, rebases, or merge messages. Pick one you already use.

```bash
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
```

Or:

```bash
git config --global core.editor "vim"
```

To make new repositories start on `main`:

```bash
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
```

> **Note:** This affects only future `git init` repositories. Existing repositories keep their current branch names until you rename them.

## Reading a `.gitconfig` File

A `.gitconfig` file is a simple INI-style file.

```ini
[user]
  name = Vishvesh Patel
  email = vishvesh@example.com
[core]
  editor = code --wait
[init]
  defaultBranch = main
```

You can edit it directly or let `git config` write the entries for you.

## Useful Git Aliases

Aliases turn longer commands into shorter ones.

Basic examples:

```bash
git config --global alias.st status
git config --global alias.co checkout
git config --global alias.br branch
git config --global alias.ci commit
```

That lets you run:

```bash
git st
git co main
git br
```

### Pretty Log Alias

A compact history view is one of the most useful aliases you can add.

```bash
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --decorate --all"
```

Then run:

```bash
git lg
```

### Workflow Aliases

A few more practical shortcuts:

```bash
git config --global alias.last "log -1 HEAD"
git config --global alias.unstage "restore --staged"
git config --global alias.amend "commit --amend"
```

Aliases should make common work faster, not hide commands you do not understand.

## Using a Global Ignore File

Some files should stay out of `git status` in every repository, such as:

- `.DS_Store`
- editor folders like `.vscode/`
- swap files
- local-only secret files

Create a personal ignore file:

```bash
touch ~/.gitignore_global
```

Example contents:

```gitignore
.DS_Store
.vscode/
*.swp
.env.local
```

Tell Git to use it:

```bash
git config --global core.excludesfile ~/.gitignore_global
```

This keeps machine-specific clutter out of all repositories without editing each project's `.gitignore`.

## A Simple Starter Setup

```bash
git config --global user.name "Vishvesh Patel"
git config --global user.email "vishvesh@example.com"
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
git config --global init.defaultBranch main
git config --global core.excludesfile ~/.gitignore_global
git config --global alias.st status
git config --global alias.co checkout
git config --global alias.br branch
git config --global alias.lg "log --oneline --graph --decorate --all"
```

## What You Should Remember

Git configuration lives at **system**, **global**, and **local** levels. Set your identity, choose a comfortable editor, define `main` as the default branch for new repositories, add a few aliases, and use a global ignore file for OS and editor clutter. Small config improvements make Git easier every day.

## Test Your Understanding

Do not alias destructive commands to short names; a two-character alias for `reset --hard` is an accident waiting to happen.

**What is a global gitignore and why use one?**

A `.gitignore` in the repository describes what that project should not track, and belongs in version control. A global ignore file, set with `git config --global core.excludesfile ~/.gitignore_global`, covers things specific to *you*: `.DS_Store`, editor directories such as `.idea/` and `.vscode/`, and local scratch files. The distinction matters as courtesy: your colleagues on other systems should not have to carry ignore rules for your operating system and editor.

**What Git settings should everyone change from the defaults?**

Four are worth setting immediately. `init.defaultBranch main`, so new repositories match what hosting platforms expect. `pull.rebase true`, which stops a plain `git pull` littering history with merge commits. `fetch.prune true`, so branches deleted upstream disappear from your local list. And `core.editor` set to something you can exit, which spares you meeting Vim unexpectedly. Adding `rerere.enabled true` pays for itself the first time you rebase through the same conflict twice.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What is a Git submodule?

A submodule is a reference from one repository to a specific commit of another. The parent repository records the child's URL in .gitmodules and the exact commit in its tree, not the files themselves. That pinning is the feature: the parent always checks out a known version of the dependency rather than whatever the other repository's main happens to be. It is also the source of most confusion, because the submodule is a separate repository with its own history, branches and remote.
Why is my submodule directory empty after cloning?

Because a plain git clone records the submodule but does not fetch its contents. Clone with git clone --recurse-submodules <url>, or fix an existing clone with git submodule update --init --recursive. Setting git config --global submodule.recurse true makes clone, pull and checkout handle submodules automatically, which removes an entire category of "it works on my machine" from a team using them.
How do I update a submodule to the latest commit?

Two different operations, easily conflated. git submodule update --init --recursive checks out the commit the parent has pinned. This is what you want after pulling someone else's change. git submodule update --remote fetches the submodule's tracked branch and moves the pin to its newest commit, which is a change to the parent repository and must be committed there. Running the second when you meant the first is how a submodule silently jumps versions.
Why is my submodule in a detached HEAD state?

Because that is by design: the parent pins a commit, not a branch, so the submodule is checked out at that exact commit with no branch attached. Committing there produces work that belongs to no branch. If you intend to make changes, cd into the submodule and git switch main (or the relevant branch) first, then commit and push in the submodule, and only afterwards commit the new pin in the parent.
What is the difference between Git submodules and subtrees?

Submodules keep the dependency as a separate repository and store only a pointer, which keeps histories clean and requires every contributor to understand submodule commands. Subtrees copy the dependency's files into the parent repository, so a normal clone gets everything and no extra commands are needed, at the cost of merging the other project's history into yours and a fiddlier update path. Subtree is kinder to contributors; submodule is stricter about separation.
Should I use submodules at all?

Only when you genuinely need to pin another repository at a known commit and cannot use a package manager. A published package, npm, PyPI, Go modules, a Terraform module registry, solves the same problem with far better tooling, versioning and caching. Submodules earn their place for vendored forks, shared configuration repositories, and monorepo-adjacent setups where no packaging exists. If a package manager can express the dependency, use it instead.

git-submodules.markdown:
## What Are Git Submodules?

A **Git submodule** lets one repository include another repository at a specific commit. The parent repository stores a reference to the child repository and exact commit to check out.

The parent project tracks a **pointer**.

Common use cases include shared libraries, external repositories, and components owned by another team.

> **Tip:** Use submodules when the nested code really needs its own repository lifecycle. If you mainly want easy dependency installation, a package manager is often a better fit.

## When to Use Submodules

Submodules make sense when several projects consume the same repository at different versions, ownership stays separate, and you want exact commit-level control.


## Adding a Submodule

Use `git submodule add` with a repository URL and path:

```bash
git submodule add https://github.com/example/shared-lib.git libs/shared-lib
```

This normally creates a `.gitmodules` file and a gitlink entry that records the submodule commit.

Example `.gitmodules` content:

```ini
[submodule "libs/shared-lib"]
  path = libs/shared-lib
  url = https://github.com/example/shared-lib.git
```

Commit both changes in the parent repo:

```bash
git add .gitmodules libs/shared-lib
git commit -m "Add shared-lib as a submodule"
```

## Cloning with Submodules

A normal clone does not always fetch submodule contents automatically. The safest approach is:

```bash
git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/example/platform.git
```

If you already cloned the parent repository without that flag, initialize submodules afterward:

```bash
git submodule update --init --recursive
```

> **Note:** This is one of the most common submodule mistakes. New contributors often clone the repository, see an empty nested folder, and think the repository is broken.

## Updating Submodules

There are two common update patterns.

### Syncing to the Parent Repository's Expected Version

If the parent repository changed its recorded submodule pointer, pull the parent changes and sync the submodule checkout:

```bash
git pull origin main
git submodule update --init --recursive
```

### Moving the Submodule to a New Commit

If you want to advance the submodule itself:

```bash
cd libs/shared-lib
git switch main
git pull origin main
```

Then go back to the parent repository and commit the new pointer:

```bash
cd ../..
git add libs/shared-lib
git commit -m "Update shared-lib submodule"
```

Updating the child repo is not enough. The parent repository must record the new submodule commit too.

## Helpful Commands

Useful inspection commands:

```bash
git submodule status
git diff --submodule
git status
```


## Removing a Submodule

Submodule removal is more involved than deleting a normal directory.

A common sequence is:

```bash
git submodule deinit -f libs/shared-lib
git rm -f libs/shared-lib
rm -rf .git/modules/libs/shared-lib
```

Then commit the cleanup:

```bash
git add .gitmodules
git commit -m "Remove shared-lib submodule"
```


## Common Pitfalls

### Forgetting `--recurse-submodules`

This leads to missing contents after clone.

### Detached HEAD Confusion

Submodules often check out a specific commit rather than following a branch tip automatically.

### Pointer Drift

A developer updates the submodule repository but forgets to commit the new pointer in the parent repository. Teammates then keep getting the old version.

### CI and Onboarding Friction

Automation must initialize submodules properly.

## Alternatives to Submodules

### Git Subtree

**Git subtree** brings another repository into a subdirectory, but the content is stored directly in the parent repository history.

Advantages include easier cloning and no separate initialization step. The trade-off is that syncing changes back can be less obvious.

### Package Managers

For many dependencies, package managers are simpler than submodules.

Examples:

- `npm` for JavaScript
- `pip` for Python
- Go modules for Go

Package managers usually offer easier onboarding for standard libraries.

## What You Should Remember

Submodules let a parent repository track another repository at a specific commit. They are useful for shared libraries and external repos that need independent history, but they add complexity around cloning, updating, CI, and removal. Learn the core commands, watch out for pointer updates, and remember that **git subtree** or a package manager may be easier for many projects.

## Test Your Understanding

      { id: 'd', text: 'When you need every dependency to have a detached HEAD by default' },

    correctId: 'a',
    explanation: 'The lesson pointed out that package managers such as npm or pip are often simpler for standard software dependencies. They provide version resolution and installation workflows that fit the language ecosystem better than submodules.',
    wrongExplanations: {
      b: 'Package managers usually reduce setup effort rather than increasing it.',
      c: 'Dependency versioning still matters, and package managers track versions in their own standard way.',
      d: 'Detached HEAD behavior is a submodule concept, not a reason to choose a package manager.',
    },
  }}

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is a Git submodule?**

That pinning is the feature: the parent always checks out a known version of the dependency rather than whatever the other repository's `main` happens to be. It is also the source of most confusion, because the submodule is a separate repository with its own history, branches and remote.

**Why is my submodule directory empty after cloning?**

Clone with `git clone --recurse-submodules <url>`, or fix an existing clone with `git submodule update --init --recursive`. Setting `git config --global submodule.recurse true` makes clone, pull and checkout handle submodules automatically, which removes an entire category of "it works on my machine" from a team using them.

**How do I update a submodule to the latest commit?**

This is what you want after pulling someone else's change. `git submodule update --remote` fetches the submodule's tracked branch and moves the pin to its newest commit, which is a change to the parent repository and must be committed there. Running the second when you meant the first is how a submodule silently jumps versions.

**Why is my submodule in a detached HEAD state?**

Committing there produces work that belongs to no branch. If you intend to make changes, `cd` into the submodule and `git switch main` (or the relevant branch) first, then commit and push in the submodule, and only afterwards commit the new pin in the parent.

**What is the difference between Git submodules and subtrees?**

Submodules keep the dependency as a separate repository and store only a pointer, which keeps histories clean and requires every contributor to understand submodule commands. Subtrees copy the dependency's files into the parent repository, so a normal clone gets everything and no extra commands are needed, at the cost of merging the other project's history into yours and a fiddlier update path. Subtree is kinder to contributors; submodule is stricter about separation.

**Should I use submodules at all?**

Only when you genuinely need to pin another repository at a known commit and cannot use a package manager. A published package, npm, PyPI, Go modules, a Terraform module registry, solves the same problem with far better tooling, versioning and caching. Submodules earn their place for vendored forks, shared configuration repositories, and monorepo-adjacent setups where no packaging exists. If a package manager can express the dependency, use it instead.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions
paragraphs: What makes a good Git commit message?

A short imperative summary under about 50 characters, "Fix login redirect loop", not "Fixed" or "Fixes", then a blank line, then a body explaining why the change was needed if it is not obvious. The summary appears in git log --oneline, on pull requests and in git blame, so it has to stand alone. The body is where the value is: the diff already shows what changed, and only the message can record the reasoning, the alternative you rejected, or the ticket that prompted it.
Why should commit messages use the imperative mood?

Because Git itself does. Its generated messages read "Merge branch 'main'" and "Revert 'Add caching'", so an imperative summary sits consistently alongside them. The practical test is that the message should complete the sentence "If applied, this commit will…", "Add rate limiting" reads correctly, "Added rate limiting" does not. It is a convention rather than a rule, and its real benefit is consistency: a log where every line is phrased the same way is far quicker to scan.
What are Conventional Commits and do I need them?

A format that prefixes the summary with a type and optional scope: feat(auth): add password reset, fix: handle empty cart, chore(deps): bump axios. The point is machine readability. Tooling can derive a changelog and the next semantic version from the log without anyone maintaining either by hand. You need them if you want automated releases or generated changelogs. If you do not, the discipline still helps, but plain clear messages are perfectly adequate.
How do Conventional Commits map to semantic versioning?

fix: produces a patch bump, feat: a minor bump, and a breaking change a major bump. A breaking change is marked either with ! after the type, feat!: drop Node 18 support, or a BREAKING CHANGE: footer in the body. Tools such as semantic-release read the commits since the last tag, work out the highest bump implied, then tag the release and write the changelog. That is why the format is strict: the version number is derived from it.
How do I change a commit message I already pushed?

git commit --amend rewrites the most recent message, but amending changes the commit hash, so a pushed commit then needs git push --force-with-lease. That is acceptable on your own feature branch and not on a shared one, where everyone who pulled is left on a commit that no longer exists. For older commits, git rebase -i HEAD~n and marking them reword does the same job with the same caveat. On main, the honest answer is to leave it.
How do I enforce commit message rules across a team?

Use commitlint with a commit-msg hook, installed through Husky so the hook lives in the repository and arrives with a clone. Raw .git/hooks files are not version-controlled and so never reach anyone else. That rejects a badly formatted message before the commit is created. Back it up with a server-side check in CI, since local hooks can be skipped with --no-verify; a pull request check that validates the commits is what actually makes the convention stick.

git-commit-messages.markdown:
## Why Good Commit Messages Matter

A commit message is part of your project's long-term memory. It explains why a change exists and helps later readers understand what happened without opening every file diff first.

Good messages improve:

- history review
- `git blame` investigations
- changelog generation
- release notes
- team communication

A weak message like `fix stuff` quickly becomes useless. A stronger message like `fix(auth): handle expired refresh tokens` gives useful context immediately.

> **Tip:** Write commit messages for the person reading them months later, not just for the moment you type them.

## The 7 Rules of a Great Commit Message

A widely used set of guidelines includes these rules:

1. Separate subject from body with a blank line
2. Keep the subject around 50 characters
3. Capitalize the subject line
4. Do not end the subject with a period
5. Use the imperative mood
6. Wrap the body near 72 characters
7. Explain **what** and **why** in the body

Example:

```text
Add validation for release tag names

Reject tag names that do not match the release policy. This prevents
invalid CI/CD releases from being published accidentally.
```

### Imperative Mood

Subjects like `Add`, `Fix`, and `Refactor` read naturally after the phrase "If applied, this commit will...".

## Good vs Bad Messages

Bad examples:

```text
stuff
misc fixes
updated files
```

Better examples:

```text
docs: clarify GitHub workflow steps
fix(ci): restore cache key for Node 22 builds
feat(api): add pagination to audit log endpoint
```

The better versions are specific and searchable.

## Conventional Commits

**Conventional Commits** define a standard format that both people and tooling can understand.

Basic pattern:

```text
type(scope): description
```

Common types include:

- `feat:`
- `fix:`
- `docs:`
- `chore:`
- `refactor:`
- `test:`
- `build:`
- `ci:`

Examples:

```text
feat(auth): add SSO login flow
fix(ui): prevent navbar overlap on mobile
docs(git): add submodule troubleshooting section
```

### Breaking Changes

A breaking change can be marked with `!` or with a `BREAKING CHANGE:` note in the body.

```text
feat(api)!: rename userId field to accountId

BREAKING CHANGE: Clients must send accountId instead of userId.
```

> **Note:** Conventional Commits are most useful when the whole team follows the same format and a hook or CI job validates it.

## Conventional Commits and Semantic Versioning

Conventional Commits connect well to **semantic versioning**:

- **MAJOR** for breaking changes
- **MINOR** for backward-compatible features
- **PATCH** for backward-compatible fixes

A common mapping is:

- `feat:` â minor bump
- `fix:` â patch bump
- `BREAKING CHANGE:` or `!` â major bump

That makes commit history useful for release automation.

## Helpful Tools

### commitlint

`commitlint` checks whether commit messages follow your rules.

```bash
npm install --save-dev @commitlint/cli @commitlint/config-conventional
```

Example config:

```bash
cat > commitlint.config.js <<'EOF'
module.exports = { extends: ['@commitlint/config-conventional'] };
EOF
```

Test a message:

```bash
echo "fix: correct cache key" | npx commitlint
```

Teams often run this from a `commit-msg` hook.

### semantic-release

`semantic-release` reads structured commit history and automates versioning and release notes.

```bash
npm install --save-dev semantic-release
```

A common pattern is:

1. developers write Conventional Commits
2. `commitlint` validates them
3. CI runs `semantic-release` on `main`
4. versioning and changelogs are generated automatically

## What You Should Remember

Good commit messages make history easier to search, review, debug, and release. The seven classic rules improve clarity, while **Conventional Commits** provide a machine-readable format that works well with tools like **commitlint** and **semantic-release**. Better commit messages are a small habit with long-term payoff.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What makes a good Git commit message?**

A short imperative summary under about 50 characters, "Fix login redirect loop", not "Fixed" or "Fixes", then a blank line, then a body explaining *why* the change was needed if it is not obvious. The summary appears in `git log --oneline`, on pull requests and in `git blame`, so it has to stand alone. The body is where the value is: the diff already shows what changed, and only the message can record the reasoning, the alternative you rejected, or the ticket that prompted it.

**Why should commit messages use the imperative mood?**

Because Git itself does. Its generated messages read "Merge branch 'main'" and "Revert 'Add caching'", so an imperative summary sits consistently alongside them. The practical test is that the message should complete the sentence "If applied, this commit willâ¦", "Add rate limiting" reads correctly, "Added rate limiting" does not. It is a convention rather than a rule, and its real benefit is consistency: a log where every line is phrased the same way is far quicker to scan.

**What are Conventional Commits and do I need them?**

A format that prefixes the summary with a type and optional scope: `feat(auth): add password reset`, `fix: handle empty cart`, `chore(deps): bump axios`. The point is machine readability. Tooling can derive a changelog and the next semantic version from the log without anyone maintaining either by hand. You need them if you want automated releases or generated changelogs. If you do not, the discipline still helps, but plain clear messages are perfectly adequate.

**How do Conventional Commits map to semantic versioning?**

`fix:` produces a patch bump, `feat:` a minor bump, and a breaking change a major bump. A breaking change is marked either with `!` after the type, `feat!: drop Node 18 support`, or a `BREAKING CHANGE:` footer in the body. Tools such as semantic-release read the commits since the last tag, work out the highest bump implied, then tag the release and write the changelog. That is why the format is strict: the version number is derived from it.

**How do I change a commit message I already pushed?**

`git commit --amend` rewrites the most recent message, but amending changes the commit hash, so a pushed commit then needs `git push --force-with-lease`. That is acceptable on your own feature branch and not on a shared one, where everyone who pulled is left on a commit that no longer exists. For older commits, `git rebase -i HEAD~n` and marking them `reword` does the same job with the same caveat. On `main`, the honest answer is to leave it.

**How do I enforce commit message rules across a team?**

Use commitlint with a `commit-msg` hook, installed through Husky so the hook lives in the repository and arrives with a clone. Raw `.git/hooks` files are not version-controlled and so never reach anyone else. That rejects a badly formatted message before the commit is created. Back it up with a server-side check in CI, since local hooks can be skipped with `--no-verify`; a pull request check that validates the commits is what actually makes the convention stick.
